stages.title: Intermediate music theory
stages.hook: Why does A minor use exactly the same notes as C major, yet sounds so different?
explain: Every major key has a relative minor that shares its key signature. The relative minor starts on the sixth note of the major scale, three semitones below the major tonic: C major and A minor, G major and E minor, F major and D minor. Same notes, but a different home note, so a different centre of gravity.

The circle of fifths arranges keys a perfect fifth apart. Going clockwise adds one sharp each step (C, G, D, A, E, B, F♯) and going anticlockwise adds one flat (C, F, B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭). Minor scales come in forms: natural (A B C D E F G), harmonic (raises the 7th: G♯) and melodic (raises 6th and 7th going up). Raising the 7th gives a leading note that pulls to the tonic.

Modes are scales built on other degrees of the major scale. Dorian (D to D on white keys) is minor with a raised 6th; Mixolydian (G to G) is major with a flat 7th. Compound metres such as 6/8, 9/8 and 12/8 divide the beat into three, and transposition moves a whole piece by one interval.

example.q: Find the relative minor of E♭ major.
steps: The relative minor starts on the sixth note of the major scale.
E♭ major: E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C. The sixth note is C.
So the relative minor is C minor.

stages.title: Harmony and counterpoint
stages.hook: How can two melodies sound together without turning into a clash, as in a Bach fugue?
explain: Harmony is built from chords that move in a logical way. Triads can be inverted: root position puts the root in the bass (C E G), first inversion puts the third in the bass (E G C) and second inversion the fifth (G C E). Adding the seventh above the root gives a seventh chord such as G7 (G B D F), whose tension wants to resolve to C.

Counterpoint is the art of combining independent melodic lines. The word comes from the Latin punctus contra punctum, note against note. The main principle is good voice leading: lines move smoothly, mostly by step, and prefer contrary motion (one up, one down) so each stays independent. In traditional counterpoint parallel perfect fifths and octaves are avoided because they make two voices sound like one.

Johann Sebastian Bach (1685–1750) is famous for counterpoint, especially fugues, in which a subject is introduced in one voice and imitated by others. Counterpoint also appears in many traditions, from medieval chant to jazz ensembles and polyphonic singing in Georgia and Central Africa.

stages.title: Musical arrangement
stages.hook: The same song can be a quiet guitar tune, a full orchestral piece or a dance remix. What changes?
explain: Arranging is deciding how an existing piece is presented: which instruments play which parts, in what range and texture, and how the music builds. The arranger keeps the song's melody and harmony but chooses the setting, tempo, feel and structure.

Key tools are instrumentation (who plays), texture (how many lines and how dense), register (high or low), dynamics and form (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro). A typical rhythm section of drums, bass and chords gives pulse and harmony, with melody instruments or voices on top. Contrast between sections stops a repeated chorus from feeling flat.

Practical rules: give each instrument its own space in range, avoid everyone playing at once all the time, check the instruments' ranges (you cannot ask a flute for a bass line), and transposing instruments such as B♭ trumpet need parts written in their own key. Arrangers work in every genre, from big band charts to film scores and electronic production.

stages.title: Improvisation
stages.hook: A player invents music on the spot, in front of an audience. How can that work without a plan?
explain: Improvisation is composing in the moment. It is not random: improvisers know the scales, chords and style, and use their ears. Many traditions have it: jazz, blues, Indian classical music, Arabic taqsim, flamenco, and Baroque keyboard players who ornamented a bass line.

A good starting tool is the pentatonic scale. C major pentatonic is C D E G A, and A minor pentatonic is A C D E G; they sound good over many chords. The blues scale adds a "blue note", the flattened fifth (A C D E♭ E G in A). Other techniques: play chord tones on strong beats, repeat and vary a short motif, use call and response (answer a phrase with another) and leave space.

Beginners can try three steps: listen, copy a simple riff, then change one thing at a time (rhythm, order, octave). Mistakes become part of the music when they are repeated or resolved. Practise over a backing track or a drone, and record yourself to hear what works.

stages.title: Ensemble performance
stages.hook: Why do orchestras need a conductor, but a jazz trio does not?
explain: Ensemble performance means making music as a team. The key skills are listening, matching tuning and timing, balancing volumes and following shared cues. Before playing, instruments are tuned to a common pitch, often an A at 440 Hz in many Western orchestras.

A conductor beats time, cues entries and shapes dynamics and style; small groups such as a string quartet use eye contact and breathing for cues. Every player needs to know their role: melody, accompaniment or rhythm. Balance means the melody is heard over the accompaniment; if you cannot hear the others, you may be too loud.

Group traditions are found worldwide: West African drum ensembles, gamelan orchestras in Indonesia, Japanese taiko drumming, mariachi bands in Mexico and brass bands in many countries. Rehearsal methods include practising parts alone, then slowly together, marking tricky spots and recording the group.

stages.title: Pop, rock and rock-and-roll
stages.hook: How did a mix of blues, gospel and country in the American South in the early 1950s change popular music around the world?
explain: Pop is short for popular music: music made for a wide audience, usually with short songs, strong melodies, clear hooks and a verse-chorus form. It changes with technology and fashion, from radio and records to streaming and social media. Pop today is global: Afrobeats from Nigeria and Ghana, K-pop from South Korea and Latin pop all reach worldwide audiences.

Rock and roll emerged in the United States in the early 1950s, drawing on rhythm and blues, gospel, blues and country. Artists such as Chuck Berry, Little Richard, Fats Domino and Elvis Presley made it famous. Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a gospel singer and guitarist, was a major influence. Its sound used electric guitar, bass, drums and a strong backbeat on beats 2 and 4.

Rock grew from rock and roll in the 1960s. Bands such as the Beatles from Liverpool and the Rolling Stones led the British Invasion, and rock developed styles from folk rock and psychedelic rock to hard rock and punk. Rock typically features distorted electric guitars, a powerful rhythm section and a focus on live performance. Both pop and rock have always borrowed from Black American music and from many other traditions.

stages.title: Country, reggae and R&B
stages.hook: A guitar chopping on the offbeat in Kingston, a fiddle in Tennessee and a voice in Detroit: what do these have in common?
explain: Country music grew from folk, blues and gospel traditions in the southern United States. Typical instruments are acoustic guitar, fiddle, banjo and pedal steel guitar; songs tell stories about daily life. Nashville became a centre, and artists such as Hank Williams, Johnny Cash, Loretta Lynn and Dolly Parton shaped the genre.

Reggae developed in Jamaica in the late 1960s from ska and rocksteady, with influence from Jamaican mento and American rhythm and blues. Its sound has a prominent bass line, rhythm guitar or keys chopping on the offbeat, and a slow-to-medium tempo with a drum accent often falling on the third beat (one drop). Bob Marley and the Wailers brought reggae to the world, and its messages often concern justice, community and hope.

Rhythm and blues (R&B) is a term for African American popular music that began in the 1940s, combining blues, gospel and jazz with a strong beat. Motown, founded in Detroit in 1959 by Berry Gordy, and Stax in Memphis made soul music famous; Aretha Franklin was known as the Queen of Soul. Modern R&B is smoother and uses electronic production and melismatic singing, where one syllable runs over several notes.

stages.title: Jazz, blues and improvisational traditions
stages.hook: Jazz and blues both grew from the African American experience, yet jazz players change a tune every time they play it. How?
explain: The blues arose in the Deep South of the United States in the late 19th century from African American work songs, spirituals and field hollers. The 12-bar blues uses three chords (I, IV, V) and lyrics that often form an AAB pattern: a line, a repeat, and an answer. Blue notes, flattened third, fifth or seventh, give it its sound.

Jazz began in New Orleans in the early 20th century, blending blues, ragtime, brass band and African rhythmic traditions. Louis Armstrong brought virtuoso trumpet and scat singing; the swing era of the 1930s featured big bands led by Duke Ellington and Count Basie; bebop in the 1940s with Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie had fast tempos and complex harmony; Miles Davis's album Kind of Blue (1959) popularised modal jazz. Ella Fitzgerald was famous for scat singing.

Improvisation is central: players take turns soloing over a repeating chord pattern. Other improvisational traditions include Indian raga (the player explores a set of notes and rules), Arabic taqsim and Turkish makam, where musicians improvise within melodic modes, and flamenco. Each tradition has its own rules, which improvisers know deeply.

stages.title: Classical music and opera
stages.hook: A singer fills an opera house with no microphone while an orchestra plays loudly. How is that possible?
explain: Western classical music is often divided into periods. Baroque (about 1600–1750) includes Bach, Handel and Vivaldi; the Classical period (about 1750–1820) includes Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven; the Romantic period (about 1820–1900) includes Chopin, Tchaikovsky and Brahms. The Classical period favoured clear forms such as the sonata and the symphony; Romantic composers stressed emotion and bigger orchestras.

Opera is drama set to music: sung words, an orchestra, scenery and acting. It began in Italy around 1600; Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) is an early landmark. Key parts are the overture, recitative (speech-like singing that moves the story along), arias (solo songs expressing emotion), ensembles and chorus. Voice types are soprano, mezzo-soprano, tenor, baritone and bass.

Famous operas include Mozart's The Magic Flute (1791), Verdi's La traviata (1853) and Puccini's La bohème (1896). Opera singers train to project without amplification by using breath support and resonance in the head and chest. Many cultures have sung drama too, such as Chinese opera (for example, Beijing opera), which combines singing, speech, acrobatics and costume.
